About: Electric & Magnetic Fields Under a Boost

Source

Lecture
19 — The Lorentz force & E/B mixing
Simulation
Electric & magnetic fields under a boost (lecture-demo mode)
Concept
E and B are frame-dependent facets of one field; a pure external magnetic field in the lab becomes electric and magnetic for a moving observer.
Serves
Field-transformation intuition; electric and magnetic contributions to the Lorentz force; transverse-force consistency across frames.
Inquiry
In this instantaneous snapshot, how do Bella's fields and the force on a test charge change as her velocity relative to Alice changes?
Misconception
"If Alice sees no electric field, no other inertial observer can see one." — In normalized field units, Bella measures E′y/(cB₀) = γv(v/c), which reverses when v reverses.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Alice's lab

Let’s start in Alice’s lab. A test charge q moves at u = 0.50c along +x through a uniform external field. In Alice's lab frame the electric field is zero and the magnetic field is B₀ = 1 into the page, so the force on the charge is purely magnetic, F = q u × B, pointing up for q > 0.

Now meet Bella: she moves along the same x-axis at a signed velocity v relative to Alice.

2 · Predict — Bella's electric field

Here’s the first puzzle. Alice measures no electric field anywhere in this region. What electric field do you think Bella measures as she moves along +x?

3 · Predict — and the magnetic field?

Now for the magnetic side. Bella also measures a magnetic field. Compared with Alice’s B₀ into the page, what do you think it is?

4 · Predict — a frame with no magnetic field?

Let’s push it further. Switch to Bella and sweep v/c across its full range. Do you think there’s a frame in which the magnetic field vanishes, leaving a purely electric field?

5 · Predict — the force at v/c = +0.50

One last experiment. Set Bella’s velocity to v/c = +0.50, matching the charge’s own u/c. Alice measures a force of 0.500 on the charge. What do you think Bella measures?

6 · Two views of one field

So here’s the big picture. Alice’s pure magnetic field and Bella’s mixed E′ and B′ are one field read from two frames: electric and magnetic are observer-dependent labels, not two separate things.

And what every observer agrees on is E² − c²B², here −c²B₀² — and because it is negative, no frame can remove the magnetic field.

The Physics

E and B under a boost · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A test charge crosses a uniform magnetic field. This sim reads that single instant from two inertial frames, Alice's lab and Bella's moving frame, and prints the fields and the force each observer measures. It shows how a field and a force are described by two observers in relative motion.

What you'll learn

  • How the fields Bella measures depend on her velocity v.
  • How the charge's speed and the force on it are measured in each frame.
  • Which quantities differ between the two frames, and which are the same for both.
  • How to read the two columns of the Readouts panel side by side.
The charge and Bella both move along x. The field is the same uniform B₀ everywhere.

What's on screen

  • Test charge q (amber disc), with its velocity as an amber arrow labelled u or u′.
  • B field (blue ⊗ lattice, into the page). Layer: Show B.
  • E field (purple arrows). Layer: Show E.
  • Net force on q (pink arrow, labelled |F| or |F′|). Layer: Show force.
  • Readouts panel: one block per frame, with E, B, the force, and two green rows (see section 07).
See itShow Alice's frame with the B and force layers on. Watch for: a blue ⊗ lattice, no purple arrows, and a pink arrow pointing up, labelled |F| = 0.500.

03

In Alice's frame the force is magnetic

A charge q with velocity u feels the Lorentz force F = q(E + u × B): an electric part qE and a magnetic part q u × B.

In Alice's lab the electric field is zero, so only the magnetic part is left:

Alice's frame in the sim's symbols (c = 1).
  • For q = +1 the force is Fy = quB₀ = +0.500, pointing up.
  • It is perpendicular to u, so it bends the path and does no work on the charge.
  • Changing the sign of q reverses the force and leaves its size alone.
See itSet the charge to q = −1 in Alice's frame. Watch for: the pink arrow flipping to point down, with the same size, |F| = 0.500.
04

A boost mixes E and B

Bella moves along +x at velocity v relative to Alice. Her fields follow from Alice's, with γv = 1/√(1 − v²/c²):

Components along the boost are unchanged. Only the perpendicular parts mix.
  • The mixing terms v × B and v × E are perpendicular to v, so nothing new appears along the boost.
  • Alice has E = 0 and B = −B₀ẑ. Bella therefore measures E′y = γv(v/c)B₀ and B′z = −γvB₀ (E in units of cB₀).
  • At v/c = +0.50, γv = 1.155, so E′y = +0.577 and B′z = −1.155.
  • Reversing v reverses E′y but not B′z, since γv is the same for ±v.
Boost along x, B into the page: E′ is transverse and flips with v.
Key idea. E and B are parts of one field. A boost mixes them, so how much of it is "electric" depends on the observer.
See itSwitch to Bella at v/c = +0.50 with the E and B layers on. Watch for: purple E′ arrows pointing up between the ⊗, and E′y = +0.577 in the readout.
See itNow reverse the boost to v/c = −0.50. Watch for: the purple arrows flipping to point down, while B′z stays −1.155.
05

Bella's fields and speed change with v

In the sim's units (c = 1, B₀ = 1), the quantities Bella reads are:

E in units of cB₀, B in units of B₀, c = 1.
  • Both fields grow with |v| and have no limit as |v| → c (the sim stops at 0.9). Their ratio stays fixed: |E′|/(c|B′|) = |v|/c, always below 1.
  • The charge's speed changes too. It follows the velocity-addition rule above: u′ = 0 at v = u, u′ = +0.80c at v/c = −0.50, and |u′| never reaches c.
  • At v = 0 Bella is Alice: E′ = 0, B′ = −B₀, u′ = u.
See itPush Bella to v/c = +0.90. Watch for: E′y and B′z both larger than at +0.50, with E′y still smaller than |B′z|.
06

The force depends on the frame

The force is dp/dt, and a boost changes both dp and dt. For a force perpendicular to u, as here:

Left: the force transform. Right: two field invariants (section 07).
  • At v/c = +0.50: 0.500 / (1.155 × 0.75) = 0.577. At v/c = −0.50: 0.500 / (1.155 × 1.25) = 0.346. The force points along the same ±y in both frames; only its size changes.
  • Bella adds her own electric and magnetic parts: F′ = qE′y − qu′B′z. At v = u, u′ = 0, so the magnetic part vanishes and the force is purely electric: F′ = qE′y = 0.577.
v/c q

See itNow try Bella at v/c = −0.50. Watch for: |F′| = 0.346 for Bella against |F| = 0.500 for Alice.
07

What every observer agrees on

Some quantities have the same value in both frames. The sim prints two of them in green.

  • E · B = 0 in both frames: E′ points along y and B′ along z.
  • E² − c²B² = −c²B₀², printed as −1.000 at every v and q. A negative value means c²B² exceeds E²: the field is magnetically dominated.
  • No frame is purely electric. The invariant stays negative, so B never vanishes. Equivalently, |E′|/(c|B′|) = |v|/c < 1.
  • The four-force magnitude. Here F ⊥ u in each frame, so the time component is zero and the magnitude is γu|F| = 0.577|q|, the same in both panels.
The four-force dpμ/dτ, and its magnitude in each frame.
See itTry the extreme setting v/c = −0.90 with q = −2. Watch for: E² − c²B² still reading −1.000 in both frames, and the four-force magnitude reading 1.155 in both.
08

Where it matters

A current-carrying wire: the same pull on a moving charge, magnetic in the lab and electric in the charge's own frame.
  • Wires and motors. A current-carrying wire is neutral in the lab, so it pulls a moving charge by a magnetic force. In the charge's frame the electrons and the ions are contracted by different amounts, the wire carries a net charge, and the same pull is electric.
  • Accelerator magnets. In a particle's own rest frame a magnet's field acts as a purely electric force on it (u′ = 0), as in the sim at v = u.
  • Magnetically dominated plasmas. Pulsar magnetospheres and the solar corona are commonly modelled with E · B = 0 and c²B² > E², the same class as the field in this sim.
Go deeper: the size of the wire's net charge
  • In the charge's frame, the wire's net line density is λ′ = −γu u I / c², where I is the lab current.
  • Its electric force is then γu times the lab's magnetic force, matching the force transform at v = u (here 0.577 against 0.500).
  • The charge density is tiny, but copper has about 10²⁹ electrons per m³. For 1 A through 1 mm², the drift speed is only about 0.07 mm/s.
09

Summary

In one line. A boost mixes the transverse parts of E and B and changes the three-force; E · B, E² − c²B² and the four-force magnitude are the same for every observer.

Key points

  • From E = 0 and B = −B₀ẑ, Bella reads E′y = γv(v/c)B₀ (odd in v) and B′z = −γvB₀ (even in v).
  • The three-force changes by F′y = Fy/[γv(1 − uv/c²)], and its direction stays the same.
  • Here E² − c²B² = −c²B₀² < 0 in every frame, so no frame is purely electric.

Common mix-ups

  • "Alice sees no electric field, so no one does." E is not invariant: Bella measures E′y = γv(v/c)B₀.
  • "If some B became E, B must get weaker." Both transverse fields grow by γv: B′z = −1.155 against Alice's −1.000 at v/c = +0.50.
  • "Every observer measures the same force." Alice reads 0.500 and Bella 0.577 at v/c = +0.50. The invariant is the four-force magnitude, 0.577 for both.

Things to try on your own

  • Set q = −2 and v/c = −0.90. Compute |F′| from F′y = Fy/[γv(1 − uv/c²)] and compare it with the Readouts panel.
  • Use Particle rest frame and divide |F′| by |F|. Compare the ratio with γv at v/c = +0.50.
  • In Bella's frame with Show E and Show B on, sweep v/c from 0 up to +0.90 and note which arrows change.
